title: Stakeholder Mapping: Voting Patterns for the Fiscal Framework
text:
The Intersection of Data and Political-Economic Analysis
As an aspiring economist, I understand that macroeconomic models and fiscal policies do not exist in a vacuum. The approval of a major economic anchor, such as the new Fiscal Framework (PLP 93/2023), relies heavily on institutional predictability and informal alliances.
This project is a core part of my continuous learning journey in quantitative research. It represents my dedication to pushing my technical boundaries, bridging the gap between raw data science and advanced political-economic analysis.



1. Data Manipulation and Algebraic Modeling
The first step in this analysis involves accessing the Chamber of Deputies’ Open Data API to systematically scrape all roll-call votes that led to the approval of the target proposition, forming the raw voting dataset.
To map tactical alliances accurately, we must filter out procedural noise and plenary absences. I quickly learned that relying on simple vote counting often misrepresents true party behavior and strategy. To solve this, I constructed relational matrices utilizing the Jaccard Similarity Index.
Mathematically, this models the exact proportion of agreement between any two parliamentarians based on their shared votes. Since the cells of this adjacency matrix are filled with continuous similarity scores, I applied a structural threshold of 0.80 to the network. This ensures that only highly cohesive tactical alliances, where mutual voting agreement exceeds 80%, are mathematically projected onto the final topology:
\[J(A,B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}\]

Technical Note on Data Cleaning & Institutional Rules: A critical step in building the relational matrices was the rigorous treatment of missing data (NAs). Plenary absences and institutional abstentions—specifically those under Article 17 of the Chamber’s Internal Regulations—were carefully isolated. Failing to separate these procedural nuances from actual “no” votes would mathematically distort the Jaccard Index, creating false proximity between parliamentarians who were simply absent and those actively opposing the agenda.



2. Unsupervised Clustering (Louvain Algorithm)
By applying the Louvain algorithm for community detection, the model revealed the invisible behavioral caucuses within the Congress.
The results provided crucial insights for political risk assessment: the algorithm indicated a pragmatic fragmentation of the “Centrão” into two distinct negotiation masses, directly reflecting the transaction costs and the slicing of parliamentary amendments. Furthermore, it mathematically captured the opposition, highlighting the tactical union of ideological extremes (PL and PSOL) in resistance to the fiscal agenda.


3. Network Metrics and Stakeholder Identification
Using Gephi (ForceAtlas 2) for topological mapping, I extracted the Betweenness Centrality metric for the network.
This calculation successfully identified the parliamentarians acting as strategic articulators, that is the literal bridges between rival blocs. For public policy forecasting, identifying these decision-makers is vital. Because they control the flow of negotiations and information, they hold the power to unlock or stall the formation of a majority for the country’s economic agenda.
(For detailed data tables, node-level metrics, and further analytical insights, please refer to the source code repository linked below.)

(Visualization of the legislative network and ideological groupings based on roll-call votes.) 



Technologies & Tools

Languages & Packages: R (dplyr, tidyr, purrr, httr, jsonlite, igraph, etc.).
Software: Gephi (ForceAtlas 2).
Data Sources: Chamber of Deputies Open Data API.

title: Administrative Unilateralism in Latin America
text:
Scaling Up Institutional Analysis
This is a large-scale computational research investigating institutional dynamics across Latin American governments. I participate in this study as a researcher for the PEX - Network group, contributing to the project titled “Administrative Unilateralism: regulatory selectivity and presidential particularism”.
Understanding comparative political economy requires analyzing institutional rules at scale. Guided by the methodological frameworks established in current academic literature on unilateralism, this project has been a steep but highly rewarding learning curve in processing “text-as-data”.
My role focuses on the backend infrastructure and data intelligence, managing the complexities of standardizing legal structures across Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia, and Paraguay.



1. Web Scraping at Scale (150,000+ Records)
Extracting data from dynamic and often unstable government and legal portals requires resilient code. I conceptualized and automated script routines for systematic batch processing.
This involved overcoming pagination barriers, managing server request rates, and bypassing connection instabilities to successfully consolidate, for example, a unified database of over 150,000 official normative records.


2. Statistical Programming and Strict Data Validation
Cleaning and modeling large institutional databases requires extreme precision. My work encompasses the manipulation, cleaning, and modeling of these datasets, ensuring the integrity and standardization of complex data originating from multiple countries. Furthermore, I am responsible for constructing the indicators, graphs, and analytical reports necessary for the project’s broader comparative goals.
Learning Note: This ongoing research continuously teaches me the critical importance of rigorous data validation and the necessity of accounting for vastly different structural standards of information across varying institutional frameworks in Latin America.


3. Natural Language Processing (NLP)
To move beyond metadata, I applied NLP techniques to decode the raw content of decrees and official acts—a crucial step for identifying regulatory selectivity.

Pre-processing & Vectorization: Transforming legal jargon into structured data.
Named Entity Recognition (NER): Automatically identifying and categorizing key political and economic actors within the texts.

Learning Note: This project marked a significant step in my technical evolution, bridging the gap between traditional web scraping and advanced computational text analysis for the evaluation of regulatory policies. For example, the process of validating regular expressions (Regex) in Argentine texts to capture regulatory selectivity required me to conduct a detailed study of the Argentine normative textual structure.



Technologies & Tools

Languages & Packages: R (dplyr, rvest, httr, jsonlite, stringi, rmarkdown, etc.); Python (Pandas, PyMuPDF/fitz, Glob, OS).
Data Sources: Various Governmental and Legal APIs.

title: Budget Gatekeepers: Federal Transfer Network in Brazil
text:
Connecting Public Finance to Political Strategy
As I delve deeper into the study of public finance, I constantly seek out complex challenges that force me to expand my quantitative toolkit. This project has been instrumental in that journey, driving me to deepen my knowledge in econometrics to investigate party bargaining power in the distribution of federal resources (Voluntary Transfers of the Union) to Brazilian municipalities.
This research goes beyond mapping; it is a rigorous political-economic analysis of how institutional “gatekeepers” control access to public funds.



1. Data Science and ETL (Panel Data)
Building a robust economic analysis requires pristine data infrastructure. I structured longitudinal panel data spanning from 2011 to 2016, containing thousands of observations.
This complex ETL pipeline integrates:

Budgetary microdata from TransfereGov/Siconv.
Territorial matching between IBGE and TSE datasets via crosswalks (utilizing the betafcc/Municipios-Brasileiros-TSE repository mapping).
Automated consumption of the Chamber of Deputies API to capture the true, fluctuating size of parliamentary caucuses.

Learning Note: Designing this architecture taught me how to handle high-dimensional relational data and merge disparate governmental sources without losing observational integrity.


2. Relational Intelligence
Unlike traditional literature, which focuses heavily on the final destination of allocated resources (the municipalities), my analytical perspective centers on the intermediaries of these transfers. To achieve this, I constructed a bipartite network mapping the exact flow of public money and subsequently projected it into a one-mode network containing only the intermediate actors (Ministries and Parliamentarians) via matrix multiplication.
This structural transformation allows for the precise application of Betweenness Centrality calculations.
Why focus on this specific metric? In public finance and political economy, the true power often lies not just with who authorizes the budget, but with who mediates it. Graph Theory allows us to map these brokers. These are the political actors who mathematically control the pathways of negotiation and information between the federal government and local municipalities. By acting as ‘bridges’ (network bottlenecks), they become the institutional gatekeepers holding the practical power to unlock, stall, or negotiate access to federal voluntary transfers.
For each year in the panel, the Betweenness Centrality is calculated based on the connection weights to identify these key intermediaries:
\[\text{Betweenness}(i) = \sum_{s \neq i \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(i)}{\sigma_{st}}\]


3. Econometric Modeling
To measure the “coalition bonus”—the interactive effect between ministerial control and and the size of the party’s caucus in the Chamber—I estimated multiple regression models (Ordinary Least Squares). This approach allowed me to mathematically quantify the impact of the budgetary decentralization generated by the institutional shock of the Impositive Amendments (EC 86/2015).



Technologies & Tools

Languages & Packages: R (electionsbr, dplyr, purr, httr, jsonlite, igraph, etc.).
Software: Gephi (ForceAtlas 2).
Data Sources: TransfereGov/Siconv; IBGE & TSE Databases (Crosswalk); Chamber of Deputies Open Data API.

title: Francisco Blasco
text:
About me
Welcome to my portfolio. I am an undergraduate student in International Economic Relations at the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG) and a researcher with the Executives, Presidents, and Cabinets Politics (PEX-Network) group, affiliated with the Center for Legislative Studies (CEL-DCP/UFMG).
I work at the intersection of political-economic analysis and Data Science. My focus is on transforming large volumes of raw, unstructured data into strategic intelligence, combining the analytical rigor of applied social sciences with the efficiency of computational solutions to interpret macroeconomic scenarios.
I have developed solid experience in automated data extraction, building web scraping pipelines and consuming APIs, as well as modeling and manipulating large databases using R and Python. Additionally, I apply computational text analysis to official documents, normative acts, and public policies. I am also trained in specific techniques for analyzing relational structures, from building sociograms to statistical network models, using specialized software such as Gephi, UCINET, and Pajek.
My goal is to continuously expand my toolkit, bridging rigorous economic and institutional theory with applied quantitative methods. I am particularly interested in economic development, Executive-Legislative relations in a comparative perspective, and the evaluation of public policies.
Ultimately, my role is to generate solid evidence, translate data into strategic intelligence, and decode complex dynamics to support decision-making in environments of uncertainty.
